messages.content: I want to reconstruct sparse-view 3D geometry with calibrated uncertainty that distinguishes unobserved structure from ambiguities caused by reflective surfaces.

The goal has two parts: reconstruct the geometry from sparse views, and make the accompanying uncertainty meaningful. In particular, uncertainty about structure that is not observed should remain distinguishable from ambiguity associated with reflective surfaces, rather than being treated as one undifferentiated kind of uncertainty.
What does calibrated uncertainty mean for the surface depths here?

The stated calibration target concerns nominal 90% surface-depth intervals. Their empirical coverage should be 85–95% on occluded regions and, separately, 85–95% on reflective regions. A nominal 90% label alone would not establish that those intervals meet the target.
So those are two separate coverage checks, not just one overall number?

Yes. The 85–95% range applies separately to occluded and reflective regions. Combining them into a single coverage figure could hide a shortfall in either category, so an aggregate figure by itself would not express the requirement.
How does that relate to distinguishing the two kinds of uncertainty?

Occluded regions relate to unobserved structure; reflective regions relate to ambiguity caused by reflective surfaces. Checking interval coverage separately keeps both cases visible when assessing calibration. It does not, by itself, specify a particular way to represent or generate those uncertainties.
Do the intervals have to achieve exactly 90% coverage?

No. They are nominal 90% intervals, while the specified acceptable coverage range is 85–95% for each of the two region types. The nominal level describes the intervals; the range describes the calibration target.
And there is also a requirement about how wide the intervals are, right?

Yes. The mean interval width should be reduced by 20% versus a calibrated ensemble, with observed-surface reconstruction error matched. In relative terms, that means targeting a mean width no greater than 80% of the calibrated ensemble’s mean width under that matched-error comparison.
Why does the comparison specify matched observed-surface reconstruction error?

It makes the width comparison conditional on comparable reconstruction error on observed surfaces. The goal is not merely to obtain narrower intervals while changing that error; the 20% reduction is assessed against the calibrated ensemble at matched observed-surface reconstruction error.
Could narrow intervals alone satisfy the goal?

No. Narrowness is only one requirement. The nominal 90% surface-depth intervals must also achieve 85–95% coverage separately on occluded and reflective regions, and the reconstruction is meant to retain the distinction between unobserved structure and reflective-surface ambiguity.
Does the 20% width reduction have to hold separately for occluded and reflective regions too?

The stated requirement explicitly calls for separate evaluation by region for coverage. It states a reduction in mean interval width versus a calibrated ensemble at matched observed-surface reconstruction error, but does not specify separate 20% width reductions for the two region types.
Is the calibrated ensemble the reference for both requirements?

It is the stated comparison baseline for mean interval width. The coverage requirement is stated directly: nominal 90% surface-depth intervals should attain 85–95% coverage on occluded regions and independently on reflective regions.
I want to be careful not to treat reflective ambiguity as though the surface were simply unobserved.

That is consistent with the goal. The distinction is between uncertainty associated with unobserved structure and ambiguity caused by reflective surfaces. Both matter to the reconstruction, but the goal asks that they remain distinguishable rather than being collapsed into the same explanation.
Can we describe this as seeking both reliable intervals and informative intervals?

Yes, with the terms tied to the stated criteria: reliable in the sense of 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% surface-depth intervals in each specified region type, and informative in the sense of a 20% lower mean interval width than the calibrated ensemble at matched observed-surface reconstruction error. Neither criterion should stand in for the other.
Does any of this say the targets have already been reached?

No. These are goals for the sparse-view 3D reconstruction and its uncertainty, not reported results. The coverage ranges and relative width reduction specify what is sought; they do not state that an evaluation has already shown it.

For the sparse-view 3D reconstruction, I propose building VisBRDF-SDF: a visibility-conditioned neural SDF posterior with view-dependent reflectance and separately calibrated occluded and reflective depth intervals.

VisBRDF-SDF names a proposed model, not a completed reconstruction. Its neural signed distance field (SDF) posterior would express uncertainty about geometry; visibility conditioning would make what is and is not visible relevant to that uncertainty. View-dependent reflectance addresses the fact that a surface’s appearance can vary with viewing direction. The depth intervals would be calibrated separately for occluded and reflective regions.
What is the role of the SDF posterior in that description?

An SDF represents geometry through signed distances to a surface. Calling it a posterior emphasizes that the proposal concerns uncertainty over the geometry, rather than only a single reconstructed surface. The description does not specify how that posterior would be parameterized or computed.
Does visibility conditioning just mean marking a region as occluded?

The proposal says the posterior is visibility-conditioned, which is broader than merely attaching an occluded label to an output. It indicates that visibility should inform the geometry posterior. It does not prescribe a particular visibility representation or conditioning mechanism.
Why include view-dependent reflectance rather than discussing geometry alone?

Because the proposal explicitly includes view-dependent reflectance alongside the geometry posterior. That keeps variation in appearance with viewing direction in the model’s description, instead of implicitly attributing every appearance difference to a change in surface geometry. It does not establish how much ambiguity that component will resolve.
Are the reflective regions just another name for occluded regions?

No. Occlusion concerns structure that is not visible from the available views, whereas the reflective category concerns ambiguity associated with reflective surfaces. A depth interval for one category should not automatically be treated as calibrated for the other; VisBRDF-SDF specifically proposes separately calibrated intervals for them.
What would be separate about that calibration?

The calibration of occluded depth intervals and reflective depth intervals would be assessed and maintained separately, rather than relying solely on a pooled assessment across both categories. The proposal does not specify a calibration algorithm or say that either category is already calibrated.
Do those depth intervals represent uncertainty in color or in geometry?

They are depth intervals, so their stated target is surface depth, which concerns geometry. View-dependent reflectance is part of the proposal, but the phrase ‘occluded and reflective depth intervals’ does not turn those intervals into color intervals.
Could the reflectance component replace the need for uncertain geometry?

Not in the proposed formulation. VisBRDF-SDF includes both a neural SDF posterior and view-dependent reflectance. The posterior retains uncertainty about geometry, while the reflectance component accounts for viewing-direction-dependent appearance. The description does not claim that either component eliminates the need for the other.
Is the proposal saying every reflective surface has uncertain depth?

No. It calls for reflective depth intervals and their separate calibration; it does not assert that every reflective surface has the same degree of depth uncertainty. Nor does it specify an interval width for any individual surface.
How should I phrase the intended distinction without claiming the model has already achieved it?

You could say: ‘VisBRDF-SDF is proposed as a visibility-conditioned neural SDF posterior with view-dependent reflectance, designed to keep depth uncertainty on occluded regions distinct from depth uncertainty on reflective regions through separate interval calibration.’ That expresses the intended distinction without reporting a result.
Does the proposal itself fix the architecture, training procedure, or calibration method?

No. It specifies the proposed model’s defining elements and the separation of occluded and reflective depth-interval calibration. It leaves the architecture, training procedure, posterior construction, and calibration procedure unstated.
So the name is attached to the combination, not just to the reflectance part?

Yes. VisBRDF-SDF refers to the proposed combination: a visibility-conditioned neural SDF posterior, view-dependent reflectance, and separately calibrated depth intervals for occluded and reflective regions. Reducing it to only a reflectance component would omit the geometry posterior and interval-calibration aspects.
And I should keep ‘separately calibrated’ explicit?

Yes. That phrase is consequential: it makes clear that occluded and reflective depth intervals are not being treated as a single calibration category. It describes a requirement of the proposed VisBRDF-SDF approach, not evidence that calibration has already been achieved.
Can VisBRDF-SDF distinguish reflection-induced depth ambiguity from unobserved geometry when reflective surfaces partially occlude the same ray?

That is an open question for the proposal, not something its description establishes. On a ray affected by both reflection and partial occlusion, uncertainty about the visible surface’s depth may coexist with uncertainty about geometry that cannot be seen. A visibility-conditioned SDF posterior and view-dependent reflectance are intended to address those different sources, but their presence alone does not show that the resulting uncertainty can be attributed to each source separately.
Why does their sharing a ray make the distinction harder?

Because the available observations may not uniquely indicate which part of a depth ambiguity comes from reflective appearance and which part comes from missing visibility. Partial occlusion restricts what is observed, while reflection can make the visible evidence ambiguous. When both affect the same ray, a depth prediction may be uncertain for both reasons at once.
Would visibility conditioning settle which explanation is responsible?

Not necessarily. Visibility conditioning can make the posterior sensitive to what is observed or occluded, but it does not by itself guarantee a unique explanation for uncertainty on a ray that also encounters a reflective surface. The question is whether the proposed model can preserve that distinction in the overlapping case, rather than merely recognizing visibility as relevant.
And view-dependent reflectance would not automatically settle it either?

Right. View-dependent reflectance gives the proposal a way to represent appearance that changes with viewpoint. It does not, just by being included, prove that reflection-induced depth ambiguity has been separated from uncertainty about unobserved geometry where the two coincide.
Could we at least say the two sources of uncertainty are conceptually different?

Yes. Reflection-induced depth ambiguity concerns what depth should be inferred from evidence affected by a reflective surface. Unobserved geometry concerns structure for which the available views do not provide direct observation. They are different concepts, even if a particular ray does not provide enough evidence to assign all of its uncertainty cleanly to one or the other.
So an overlapping ray might be uncertain without having a single clear cause?

Exactly. The uncertainty could reflect both ambiguous evidence from reflection and a lack of observation due to occlusion. Saying that both may contribute is different from claiming that VisBRDF-SDF has successfully quantified each contribution on that ray.
VisBRDF-SDF proposes separately calibrated occluded and reflective depth intervals. Would that answer my question?

Not on its own. Separate calibration concerns how the depth intervals behave for occluded and reflective regions. Your question is more specific: when both effects occur on the same ray, can the posterior distinguish the reasons for depth ambiguity? Even well-calibrated intervals in the two region categories would not, by themselves, establish that such an attribution is identifiable or correctly made on overlapping rays.
What if a ray qualifies as both reflective and partially occluded?

Then treating ‘reflective’ and ‘occluded’ as mutually exclusive descriptions would obscure the question. The ray can involve both phenomena. The proposal does not specify how overlapping cases are categorized or how their uncertainty would be divided, so its ability to handle that case remains to be determined.
Is distinguishing them the same as predicting a narrow depth interval?

No. Interval width describes how concentrated a depth estimate is. Distinguishing the sources of ambiguity asks what accounts for the uncertainty, especially when reflection and incomplete visibility affect the same ray. A narrow interval would not demonstrate a correct distinction, and a wide interval would not reveal which source caused its width.
Could a posterior represent multiple plausible depths yet still fail to distinguish the causes?

Yes. Representing multiple plausible depths addresses uncertainty about what the geometry might be. It does not automatically identify whether those alternatives arise from reflective appearance, unobserved structure, or both. The proposed SDF posterior may express geometric uncertainty without the stated description guaranteeing that causal separation.
Does the question imply that separation is impossible?

No. It asks whether VisBRDF-SDF can achieve the distinction under a particularly difficult overlap. The proposal alone supports neither a claim of success nor a claim of impossibility. Where the observations cannot discriminate between explanations, however, a uniquely determined attribution should not be assumed.
How can I keep the question precise without assuming the answer?

You could ask: ‘When a reflective surface partially occludes the same ray, can VisBRDF-SDF distinguish depth ambiguity attributable to reflection from uncertainty about geometry left unobserved by the occlusion?’ That preserves the overlap and frames distinguishability as something to establish, not as a capability already demonstrated.
So the central concern is not whether the model contains both components, but whether their outputs remain interpretable where their effects overlap?

Yes. Having visibility conditioning and view-dependent reflectance states what the proposal includes. The unresolved issue is whether, on a ray affected by both partial occlusion and reflection, those components support a meaningful distinction between ambiguity in the observed evidence and uncertainty about unseen geometry.

My hypothesis is that visibility and specular-residual factors will distinguish mixed-ray ambiguities, while achieving 85–95% coverage per region and intervals 20% narrower than those of calibrated ensembles.

That frames a testable expectation, not an established result. The factors are hypothesized to help distinguish uncertainty about unobserved geometry from reflection-induced depth ambiguity when both affect a ray. The same hypothesis includes 85–95% coverage in each region and intervals 20% narrower than those of calibrated ensembles.
What does “mixed-ray ambiguity” mean in this hypothesis?

It refers to the overlap in the question we discussed: a reflective surface partially occludes the same ray, so reflective appearance and missing observation can both contribute to depth ambiguity. The hypothesis is that the two factors will help keep those contributions distinguishable even in that case.
How are the visibility and specular-residual factors supposed to differ conceptually?

The visibility factor is concerned with what the available views do or do not observe. The specular-residual factor is concerned with ambiguity associated with reflective appearance. Their proposed distinction mirrors the two uncertainty sources; the hypothesis does not specify their mathematical form or prove that they can separate every overlapping case.
Does “specular-residual” mean the reflective ambiguity has already been isolated?

No. It names a factor intended to help distinguish that ambiguity. Calling it a specular-residual factor does not establish that the residual is uniquely attributable to reflection, particularly on a ray that is also partially occluded.
The coverage claim says “per region.” Which regions does that refer to?

In this discussion, it refers to occluded and reflective regions separately. The hypothesis is not merely that coverage pooled across them will fall between 85% and 95%; each region has that coverage target.
And those are still the nominal 90% surface-depth intervals we have been discussing?

Yes. In the established context, the coverage target concerns nominal 90% surface-depth intervals. The hypothesized 85–95% coverage is the acceptable empirical range for those intervals in each region, not a change to their nominal level.
If a ray is both reflective and partially occluded, does “per region” mean we must force it into exactly one category?

No such rule follows from the hypothesis. Separate coverage targets for occluded and reflective regions do not, by themselves, specify how a ray belonging to both descriptions is categorized. The mixed-ray question is precisely about whether the factors can distinguish the overlapping sources of ambiguity.
Could the coverage targets be met without the factors actually distinguishing what causes an ambiguous depth?

Yes, in principle. Coverage describes whether the depth intervals contain the relevant depths at the stated rate. It does not alone demonstrate that uncertainty on a mixed ray has been attributed correctly to visibility or specular effects. The distinguishing claim is a separate part of the hypothesis.
Likewise, would being 20% narrower establish that distinction?

No. Narrower intervals concern precision relative to calibrated ensembles. Even if that width comparison held, it would not by itself establish that visibility and specular-residual factors distinguish the sources of mixed-ray ambiguity. The hypothesis asks for both properties.
Should I describe the 20% comparison as being against an uncalibrated baseline?

No. The stated comparison is against calibrated ensembles. Changing that to uncalibrated baselines would change the hypothesis. In the broader goal, the interval-width comparison is made at matched observed-surface reconstruction error.
Does the hypothesis say the intervals are exactly 20% narrower in every region or on every ray?

It says ‘20% narrower intervals than calibrated ensembles’; it does not specify a per-ray guarantee or separate 20% reductions for occluded and reflective regions. The explicitly region-specific numerical requirement is 85–95% coverage per region.
What would be an overstatement when I discuss this?

Saying that the factors already distinguish mixed-ray ambiguity, that coverage has been measured within 85–95% in each region, or that the intervals have already beaten calibrated ensembles by 20% would be an overstatement. Those are the hypothesized outcomes, not reported findings.
Can I still connect the hypothesis directly to the question about a reflective surface partially occluding a ray?

Yes. That overlap is what ‘mixed-ray ambiguities’ refers to here. You can say the hypothesis proposes visibility and specular-residual factors as a way to distinguish reflection-induced depth ambiguity from unobserved geometry in that setting, while retaining the separate coverage and interval-width targets.
So if the factors signal both sources for one ray, that would not contradict the distinction?

Not necessarily. Distinguishing the sources need not mean claiming that only one source affects each ray. For a mixed ray, acknowledging both is compatible with the hypothesis; what remains unproven is whether the factors can distinguish their respective contributions meaningfully.

To investigate the mixed-ray question, I plan to create MirrorOcclude-3V mixed-ray scenes, ablate the visibility and specular factors, then calibrate the intervals and compare regionwise coverage and width against matched-error ensembles.

That sets out an evaluation sequence. MirrorOcclude-3V would provide scenes centered on rays where reflection and occlusion overlap. Ablating the visibility and specular factors would examine their roles in the proposed distinction. After interval calibration, the plan is to compare coverage and width by region against ensembles matched for reconstruction error. None of those steps is a completed result.
What exactly is the question these scenes are meant to address?

They are meant to probe whether VisBRDF-SDF can distinguish reflection-induced depth ambiguity from uncertainty about unobserved geometry when a reflective surface partially occludes the same ray. The overlap matters: looking only at reflection or only at occlusion would not directly pose that mixed-ray question.
Does the name MirrorOcclude-3V specify how many scenes or rays I will create?
No such quantity is stated. MirrorOcclude-3V is the name given to the planned mixed-ray scenes; the plan does not supply a scene count, ray count, or scene-construction procedure.
What should I understand by ‘ablate’ here?

An ablation is a comparison that removes or changes a proposed component to examine its contribution. Here, the components named for ablation are the visibility and specular factors. The plan does not give the exact ablation configurations or predict their outcomes.
Why examine both factors instead of just reporting interval coverage?

Because interval coverage and the mixed-ray distinction address different issues. Coverage concerns how often the depth intervals contain the relevant depth within a region. Ablating the factors is aimed at understanding their contribution to distinguishing the two sources of ambiguity. Good coverage alone would not establish that distinction.
If I ablate a visibility factor, may I conclude that any change is due solely to occlusion?

The planned ablation could provide evidence about the factor’s contribution, but that conclusion would require care. The plan does not guarantee that a visibility factor affects only occlusion or that changes in a mixed-ray setting have a single explanation. It specifies what to examine, not what the comparison will show.
And the same caution applies to the specular factor?

Yes. Ablating the specular factor is relevant to reflective ambiguity, but the plan does not establish in advance that every effect of that ablation can be assigned uniquely to reflection when the same rays are partially occluded.
Where does calibration come in the sequence?

The stated order is to create the mixed-ray scenes, ablate the visibility and specular factors, then calibrate the intervals and compare their regionwise coverage and width against matched-error ensembles. Calibration is part of the plan, not something already performed.
When we say ‘regionwise coverage,’ do we mean one pooled result for all difficult rays?

No. ‘Regionwise’ calls for coverage to be examined by region rather than relying on a pooled number. In the established goal, the relevant regions are occluded and reflective regions, each with an 85–95% coverage target for nominal 90% surface-depth intervals.
Would a ray affected by both phenomena necessarily be assigned to only one of those regions?

The plan does not specify a rule for assigning overlapping rays to regions. It calls for mixed-ray scenes and regionwise comparisons, but leaves the handling of a ray that is both reflective and partially occluded unstated. Assuming the regions are mutually exclusive would add a decision that is not in the plan.
Is interval width also to be compared by region?

Yes. The plan explicitly says to compare regionwise coverage and width against matched-error ensembles. That makes both coverage and width part of the by-region comparison, without specifying a separate numerical width target for every region.
What does matching the ensembles on error protect in that comparison?

It makes the interval comparison conditional on comparable reconstruction error, rather than comparing widths across differing error levels without qualification. In the stated goal, the relevant match is observed-surface reconstruction error. The plan does not state how that matching will be carried out.
Is the ensemble comparison itself enough to tell us whether the two factors distinguish ambiguity?

Not by itself. Coverage and width comparisons assess the behavior of the depth intervals relative to the matched-error ensembles. The ablations bear on what the visibility and specular factors contribute. The mixed-ray question still requires care in interpreting whether uncertainty from reflection and unobserved geometry is actually being distinguished.
If a planned comparison shows narrower intervals, can I call the uncertainty calibrated?

Not from width alone. Calibration concerns coverage of the intervals, which is why the plan includes calibrating them and comparing regionwise coverage as well as width. Narrower intervals could fail the coverage target; the plan does not presume either result.
Should the 85–95% coverage target be read as applying to the aggregate across the MirrorOcclude-3V scenes?

The target is region-specific: 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% surface-depth intervals separately on occluded and reflective regions. An aggregate across scenes would not replace those separate checks. The plan does not give further details about aggregation within a region.
How should I describe the role of MirrorOcclude-3V without claiming it has already resolved the question?

You can describe MirrorOcclude-3V as planned mixed-ray scenes for probing the overlap between reflective depth ambiguity and unobserved geometry. The scenes, ablations, calibration, and matched-error ensemble comparisons form a proposed evaluation; they do not yet establish whether VisBRDF-SDF succeeds.
So the plan has an interpretive part and an interval-quality part?

That is a useful distinction. The mixed-ray scenes and factor ablations address the interpretive question about reflection and occlusion on the same ray. Calibrating intervals and comparing regionwise coverage and width against matched-error ensembles addresses the stated uncertainty-quality criteria. The plan includes both without claiming their outcomes in advance.

I’m moving to the evaluation activity: fit held-out regional calibrators, then run five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V visibility/specular ablations against error-matched ensembles, measuring 90% depth coverage and interval width.

That specifies what to carry out, not what the results will be. The regional calibrators are to be fitted using held-out data. The five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V runs will examine the visibility and specular factors through ablations, with error-matched ensembles as comparators. The interval measurements are coverage for nominal 90% depth intervals and their width.
When I say “regional calibrators,” which distinction should remain visible?

The distinction between occluded and reflective regions. Fitting regional calibrators keeps their depth-interval calibration separate, rather than treating a pooled calibration result as sufficient for both.
Does “held-out” tell us exactly how to partition the data?
No. It says the data used for fitting the regional calibrators are held out, but this activity does not specify the partitioning procedure or its sizes.
I don’t want “five-seed” to sound like five different scene types.
Then describe it as five-seed runs of the MirrorOcclude-3V ablations. The number refers to seeds for the runs; it does not, by itself, specify a count of scenes or scene types.
What belongs in the visibility/specular ablations?

The named factors to examine are visibility and specular factors. Ablating them lets the runs probe their contributions in the mixed-ray setting. The activity does not state the exact set of ablation configurations, so it would be premature to list specific variants as though they were fixed.
And “against error-matched ensembles” is a comparison, not another factor being ablated?

Correct. The ensembles are the comparison for the ablation runs’ interval measurements, with reconstruction error matched. The activity does not say to ablate components of the ensembles or specify the matching procedure.
Is the measured 90% depth coverage supposed to be exactly 90%?

The 90% describes the nominal depth intervals whose empirical coverage will be measured. It is not a report that measured coverage is exactly 90%. The established target is 85–95% coverage separately on occluded and reflective regions.
Could I report one coverage number across all MirrorOcclude-3V rays?

A pooled number would not replace the regional measurement called for here. The calibration is regional, and the coverage question concerns occluded and reflective regions separately. The activity does not specify how rays affected by both phenomena will be counted in those regional measurements.
What should “width” mean in the same sentence as coverage?

It is the width of the depth intervals whose coverage is being measured. Keeping the two measurements together matters: coverage assesses whether the intervals contain the relevant depths at the expected rate, while width describes how broad those intervals are.
If the intervals get narrower in an ablation run, have we shown that the factors separate reflection from occlusion?

No. A width change alone would not establish an interpretable separation of the two ambiguity sources. The ablations are meant to examine the factors’ contributions, and the coverage and width measurements assess interval behavior; interpreting mixed-ray ambiguity still requires care.
What does matching error allow me to say about the ensemble comparison?

It makes the interval comparison one against ensembles at matched reconstruction error, rather than an unqualified comparison between systems with differing errors. In the stated goal, that condition is matched observed-surface reconstruction error. It does not predict which intervals will be narrower.
Should I describe the five-seed runs as having demonstrated the hypothesis?

Not from the activity description. It says to run the ablations and measure coverage and width; it supplies no measurements or conclusions. The five seeds describe the planned runs, not evidence of an outcome.
Can you give me a compact wording that keeps the activity and its limits clear?

“Fit regional depth-interval calibrators on held-out data, and run five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V visibility/specular ablations with error-matched ensemble comparisons. Measure empirical coverage of nominal 90% depth intervals and their widths by region.” That states the work and measurements without claiming a result.
What are the reported results from the five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V evaluation?

VisBRDF-SDF achieved 91% coverage on occluded regions and 81% coverage on reflective regions. Its intervals were 12% narrower than those of the error-matched ensembles. Those are the reported coverage and width results; no per-seed figures are given.
Are the two coverage percentages for different kinds of regions?
Yes. The 91% figure is for occluded regions, and the 81% figure is for reflective regions. They are separate regional coverage measurements, not two estimates of one pooled coverage value.
How far apart are those coverage figures?
They differ by 10 percentage points: 91% on occluded regions versus 81% on reflective regions. That describes the difference in the reported coverage rates without assigning a cause to it.
These measurements concern the nominal 90% depth intervals, correct?
Correct. The evaluation measured coverage of nominal 90% depth intervals. The nominal level is 90%; the observed regional coverage figures reported here are 91% and 81%.
Can you explain ‘12% narrower’ without making it sound like a coverage result?

It is a comparison of interval widths, not of coverage rates. Relative to the error-matched ensembles’ intervals, VisBRDF-SDF’s intervals were reported as 12% narrower—equivalently, their reported comparative width is 88% of the ensemble width. That statement does not change the separate 91% and 81% coverage figures.
Does the 12% apply independently to both occluded and reflective intervals?

The evidence gives one 12% width comparison and does not report separate width reductions for occluded and reflective regions. It would add detail not present in the result to assign that percentage to each region independently.
And ‘error-matched’ refers to the ensembles used for the width comparison?
Yes. The reported 12% narrower intervals are compared against error-matched ensembles. The evidence does not give the matched error values or further details of how the matching was performed.
Could I infer what coverage the ensembles achieved from that sentence?
No. The sentence reports VisBRDF-SDF’s regional coverage and a relative interval-width comparison with the ensembles. It does not supply the ensembles’ regional coverage percentages.
Does ‘five-seed’ give us a range for the 91% or 81% figures?
No. It identifies the evaluation as five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V, but the evidence supplies only the reported coverage figures. It gives no seed-by-seed values, ranges, or variation estimates.
Can I say reflective coverage was nine percentage points below the nominal interval level?

Yes, as a numerical description: 81% is nine percentage points below the nominal 90% level. Likewise, 91% is one percentage point above it. Those comparisons do not supply any additional measurements beyond the reported percentages.
Would it be accurate to call the reflective figure 81% narrower?

No. The 81% figure is reflective-region coverage. Narrowness refers to interval width, for which the reported relative difference is 12% versus the error-matched ensembles. Keeping coverage and width distinct avoids mixing their units and meanings.
What if I want one sentence that preserves the region labels and the comparison?
“On five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V, VisBRDF-SDF achieved 91% coverage on occluded regions and 81% on reflective regions, with intervals 12% narrower than those of error-matched ensembles.”
Does that sentence imply we know the absolute depth-interval widths?
No. It reports a relative width difference, not the absolute widths of either VisBRDF-SDF’s intervals or the ensembles’ intervals. The absolute width values are not provided here.
So I should keep the coverage figures regional, and the width figure tied to its comparator?

Exactly. Report 91% for occluded regions and 81% for reflective regions, and describe the 12% narrower intervals specifically relative to error-matched ensembles. The five-seed MirrorOcclude-3V setting belongs with those reported figures.

I have a hypothesis for the mixed-ray problem: separating specular-ray modes from occlusion priors should yield 85–95% coverage regionwise and intervals at least 20% narrower than matched-error ensembles.

That is a proposed outcome, not an observed result. The separation is intended to keep ambiguity associated with specular rays distinct from uncertainty associated with occluded geometry. The hypothesis predicts two interval properties: 85–95% coverage in each relevant region and interval widths at least 20% lower than those of matched-error ensembles.
What distinction is the hypothesis making between specular-ray modes and occlusion priors?

Conceptually, specular-ray modes concern alternative depth interpretations associated with reflective appearance. Occlusion priors concern what may be inferred about geometry that is not observed. Separating them means not treating those two sources of uncertainty as interchangeable, especially when reflection and partial occlusion affect the same ray. The hypothesis does not specify their mathematical representations.
Does ‘separating’ mean that a mixed ray must be assigned to just one source of ambiguity?

No. A ray can be affected by both reflection and occlusion. The proposed separation concerns how those sources are represented or distinguished; it does not imply that every ray has exactly one source, or that one source must be ignored when both are present.
Could the specular-ray modes tell us with certainty which depth is correct?

The hypothesis does not claim that. Referring to modes allows for distinct possibilities associated with a reflective ray; it does not say that the correct depth is uniquely identifiable. The prediction is about the resulting regional coverage and interval widths, not certainty for every ray.
What should I make of the word ‘priors’ in ‘occlusion priors’?

It indicates assumptions brought to bear on geometry where observation is limited by occlusion. It does not mean that the hidden geometry has been directly observed. The hypothesis leaves the content and form of those priors unspecified.
Which regions are covered by ‘85–95% coverage regionwise’?
In this setting, the regions are occluded and reflective regions. The 85–95% coverage prediction applies separately to each, rather than only to a pooled measurement across them.
Are we still talking about nominal 90% surface-depth intervals?

Yes. The established interval target is nominal 90% surface-depth intervals. Here, 85–95% is the hypothesized empirical coverage range for those intervals in each region; it is not a new nominal interval level.
How should I read ‘at least 20% narrower’ mathematically?

For the stated width comparison, it means a mean interval width no more than 80% of the matched-error ensemble’s mean interval width. The ‘at least’ matters: the hypothesis predicts a reduction of 20% or more, not exactly 20%.
Does the width prediction say every interval must be 20% narrower?

No. It is an interval-width comparison against matched-error ensembles, not a guarantee about each individual interval or ray. Nothing here specifies that every depth interval must attain the same relative reduction.
Does it also say there must be a separate 20% width reduction in each region?

The coverage prediction is explicitly regionwise. The hypothesis does not explicitly assign a separate at-least-20% width reduction to occluded and reflective regions individually. That stronger reading should not be assumed from the wording.
Why keep ‘matched-error ensembles’ in the wording?

They are the stated comparator for interval width. Matching reconstruction error makes the predicted width reduction a comparison under comparable error, rather than an unqualified claim of narrower intervals. The hypothesis does not specify how the matching is performed.
If regional coverage falls in range, would that alone establish that the two sources of ambiguity were separated?

No. Coverage describes how frequently intervals contain the relevant surface depths. It does not, by itself, show whether uncertainty on a mixed ray was meaningfully attributed to reflective ambiguity versus unobserved geometry. The proposed separation and the interval-performance predictions are related but distinct claims.
And if intervals are at least 20% narrower, could that come at the expense of coverage?

That is possible in principle, which is why the hypothesis includes both requirements. A width reduction alone would not satisfy the predicted outcome if coverage did not also fall within 85–95% separately on occluded and reflective regions.
Does this hypothesis specify an implementation of the separation?

No. It identifies specular-ray modes and occlusion priors as the things to separate and states the expected interval outcomes. It does not fix an architecture, a procedure for separating them, or a method for calibrating the resulting intervals.
